text:
**LiFePO4 is the better choice for most people.** NMC only makes sense if you carry the unit often and rarely use it.

## Why LiFePO4 wins
- **Cycle life:** LiFePO4 stations are typically rated for 3,000-6,000 cycles to 80% capacity. NMC ratings run from about 500 to 2,500 depending on the source and model ([OutageMath](https://www.outagemath.com/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc/), [UnpluggedWatts](https://www.unpluggedwatts.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-power-station/)). With daily cycling, 500 cycles lasts about 1.4 years, while 3,000 lasts about 8.
- **Safety:** Lab studies on small cells show LiFePO4 failing more mildly. In one test an NMC cell peaked at 731°C and a LiFePO4 cell at 259°C ([OutageMath](https://www.outagemath.com/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc/)). In another, LiFePO4 released smoke without flames, but it reached thermal runaway earlier under overcharge ([UnpluggedWatts](https://www.unpluggedwatts.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-power-station/)). So LiFePO4 is not fireproof, but its failures are less violent, which matters for a unit kept indoors or in a vehicle.
- **Market:** Nearly all current mid-size and large stations are LiFePO4. One catalog lists 121 of 128 models as LiFePO4 ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc)).

## Where NMC wins
NMC cells hold more energy per kilogram, but the advantage shrinks in finished products. The inverter, case and fans weigh the same either way. In same-maker pairs, the LiFePO4 version was only slightly heavier per kWh ([OutageMath](https://www.outagemath.com/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc/)). One LiFePO4 station even beat an NMC one on Wh per pound ([UnpluggedWatts](https://www.unpluggedwatts.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-power-station/)). Compare actual specs rather than assuming the chemistry decides weight.

Cold weather is about the same for both. Most stations of either type won't charge below 32°F, so check the manual.

## Specific models
Prices and codes are from [Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/answers/portable-power-station-lifepo4-nmc-battery-chemistry-manufacturer-comparison-202), tested between Oct 21 and 24, 2026. These are affiliate links, so Dealectric is paid if you buy, at no cost to you.

| Model | Chemistry | Capacity / output | Weight | Price |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [BLUETTI Elite 200 V2](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-elite-200-v2) | LiFePO4, 6,000+ cycles | 2,073.6 Wh / 2,600 W | 24.2 kg | $899, or $854.05 with AFF5OFF |
| [BLUETTI AC180](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac180) | LiFePO4, 3,500+ cycles | 1,152 Wh / 1,800 W | ~16 kg | $499, or $474.05 with AFF5OFF |
| [ALLPOWERS P1800](https://dealectric.com/go/allpowers-p1800-1024wh) | LiFePO4, 3,000+ cycles (to 70%) | 1,024 Wh / 1,800 W | ~13 kg | $439, or $395.10 with ALLPOWERS26 |
| [ALLPOWERS S2000 Pro](https://dealectric.com/go/allpowers-s2000-pro-1451wh) | NMC, 2,500+ cycles | 1,451 Wh / 2,400 W | 13 kg | $664, or $597.60 with EXTRA10 (expires Nov 15) |

Some caveats on these:
- The S2000 Pro's price per Wh is about the same as the Elite 200 V2's after codes, so NMC isn't cheaper here.
- Its solar input is listed inconsistently (1,000 W in the spec table, 650 W in the FAQ).
- The P1800's US page contradicts itself on cycles and UPS time, and its weight comes from product images only.
- The AC180's $499 price is for the station alone.
- Another retailer lists the S2000 Pro at $1,399 as the regular price ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc)), so confirm the current price.

## How to choose
- **Daily or frequent use, home backup, van or off-grid:** LiFePO4.
- **Weekend camping with a real weight limit:** either one works, so decide on weight and price.
- **Rare outages:** either one works. Calendar aging and storage matter more than cycle count.
- **Already own a working NMC unit:** keep using it.

Check the chemistry and the cycle rating's end point (70% vs 80%) on the spec sheet before you buy. A 70% rating promises less than an 80% one with the same cycle count.
